item_description: A mobile operating system based on the Linux kernel and developed by Google with an open ecosystem of device makers.
item_facts: Android is based on the Android Open Source Project.
Google Play services are separate from the open-source core.
Device update timing depends on manufacturer, carrier and model.

item_description: A lightweight, rolling-release Linux distribution designed for users who prefer configuring their own system.
item_facts: Arch Linux uses the pacman package manager.
Its documentation is maintained in the ArchWiki.
A rolling release model provides ongoing updates rather than fixed major releases.
needs_review: Verify current installation and package-management details on Arch Linux documentation.

item_description: Google’s operating system for Chromebooks, built around web services and support for Android and Linux applications on many devices.
item_facts: ChromeOS is used primarily on Chromebook computers.
Many Chromebooks support Android apps through Google Play.
Linux development environments are available on supported devices.

item_description: A community-developed free operating system distribution that forms the basis for many other Linux distributions.
item_facts: Debian began in 1993, founded by Ian Murdock.
It supports multiple processor architectures.
Debian releases stable versions alongside testing and unstable branches.

item_description: A community Linux distribution sponsored by Red Hat and known for adopting newer open-source technologies.
item_facts: Fedora is an upstream community project for Red Hat Enterprise Linux.
It uses the DNF package manager.
Fedora offers editions tailored to workstation, server and other use cases.

item_description: A free and open-source Unix-like operating system known for performance, networking and a unified base system.
item_facts: FreeBSD descends from the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) lineage.
It includes a complete operating system rather than only a kernel.
Its license differs from copyleft licenses such as the GNU GPL.

item_description: Apple’s mobile operating system for iPhone devices.
item_facts: iOS is developed by Apple.
Apple distributes major iOS updates to supported iPhone models.
The App Store is Apple’s primary app marketplace for iOS.

item_description: A Debian-based Linux distribution maintained by Offensive Security for penetration testing and security research.
item_facts: Kali bundles security testing and forensics tools.
It is maintained by Offensive Security.
Its tools should only be used on systems where the operator has authorization.
needs_review: Verify current release details on Kali’s official site.

item_description: A Linux distribution based on Ubuntu or Debian, designed to provide a familiar desktop experience.
item_facts: Linux Mint offers Cinnamon, MATE and Xfce desktop editions.
The Cinnamon desktop is developed by the Linux Mint project.
Its main edition is based on Ubuntu, while LMDE is based directly on Debian.

item_description: A named version of Apple’s desktop operating system for Mac computers.
item_facts: macOS is developed by Apple.
Apple releases macOS versions with compatibility limited to supported Mac models.
The Tahoe release name and its features are version-specific.

item_description: A Linux distribution built around the Nix package manager and declarative system configuration.
item_facts: NixOS uses configuration files to describe system state.
The Nix package manager supports reproducible package environments.
System generations allow users to roll back to earlier configurations.
needs_review: Verify current terminology and capabilities using NixOS documentation.

item_description: A free Unix-like operating system project that emphasizes correctness, security and code review.
item_facts: OpenBSD is developed by a volunteer community.
The project provides the OpenSSH suite, which is also used by many other systems.
OpenBSD releases a new version approximately every six months.
needs_review: Verify current release cadence and project claims on OpenBSD’s official site.

item_description: Oracle’s enterprise Unix operating system, descended from Sun Microsystems’ Solaris.
item_facts: Solaris originated at Sun Microsystems.
Oracle acquired Sun Microsystems in 2010.
Solaris includes technologies such as ZFS and DTrace, which originated in the Solaris ecosystem.
needs_review: Verify current support, licensing and feature availability through Oracle documentation.

item_description: A security-focused desktop operating system that isolates activities in separate virtual machines called qubes.
item_facts: Qubes OS uses Xen virtualization.
It separates domains such as personal, work and untrusted browsing.
Isolation reduces some risks but does not eliminate all security threats.
needs_review: Verify current architecture and threat-model wording on Qubes OS documentation.

item_description: A commercial enterprise Linux distribution from Red Hat, designed for server, cloud and workstation deployments.
item_facts: RHEL uses RPM packages and the DNF package manager.
Red Hat publishes long support lifecycles for major versions.
Some source code is available through Red Hat and community channels under open-source licenses.

item_description: Valve’s Linux-based operating system designed for Steam gaming devices, including Steam Deck.
item_facts: SteamOS is based on Arch Linux in the current Steam Deck generation.
It uses the KDE Plasma desktop environment in desktop mode.
Compatibility with Windows games is supported in part through Proton.
needs_review: Verify current base distribution and software versions using Valve documentation.

item_description: A portable Linux operating system designed to help preserve privacy and anonymity when browsing.
item_facts: Tails routes internet connections through Tor by default.
It is designed to leave as little trace as possible on the computer used.
Tails cannot protect against every threat, such as compromised hardware or user error.
needs_review: Verify current security design and limitations using official Tails documentation.

item_description: A widely used Linux distribution developed by Canonical and a global community.
item_facts: Ubuntu is based on Debian.
Canonical publishes regular releases, including long-term support versions.
It is available for desktops, servers, cloud environments and Internet of Things devices.

item_description: Microsoft’s desktop operating system released in 2021, with a modernized interface and hardware requirements.
item_facts: Windows 11 requires supported hardware including TPM 2.0 for standard installation requirements.
Microsoft provides feature updates and security updates through Windows Update.

item_facts: Windows Server editions include server roles such as Active Directory Domain Services.
